Distance to the nearest T-cell-positive bin is consequently depth-driven, and on an 8 µm grid it is also coarsely discretised. We therefore defined the outcome as the number of T-cell transcripts divided by the total UMI within a 48 µm radius of each bin, excluding the bin itself, expressed per 1,000 UMI. Normalising by local UMI removes the direct effect of library size on the outcome. It does not remove every path: the denominator also depends on local cell density and on the tumour, stromal and immune composition of the neighbourhood, so the ratio can move for reasons other than the number of T cells present. Each CLEC10A-positive myeloid bin was then matched, without replacement and within section, to a CLEC10A-negative myeloid bin with the same myeloid count (capped at six) and the same log total UMI rounded to one decimal place. Matching was verified to equalise not only the bin's own depth but the depth of its neighbourhood (ratio of mean neighbourhood UMI, CLEC10A-positive to matched negative, 0.963 to 1.003 across sections). Matched pairs were compared within section as paired differences (assignments in Supplementary Table S8), summarised by the Hodges-Lehmann estimator. Two dependencies rule out treating bins or sections as independent. Neighbourhoods of 48 µm overlap, so between 70% and 100% of analysed bins per section lie within 96 µm of another analysed bin; and two of the six sections come from one patient, leaving five independent patients. Rank tests on so few units are also bounded: with five units the smallest attainable two-sided exact P is 0.0625, so such a test cannot reach conventional significance however large the effect.

Uncertainty was therefore obtained by a hierarchical bootstrap with 4,000 draws. Patients were resampled with replacement; within each sampled patient's section or sections, contiguous square tiles of bins were resampled with replacement and the paired statistic recomputed, so that local spatial structure is preserved rather than broken by exchanging individual bins. Tiles of 25 bins (200 µm) were used, with 12 and 50 bins as sensitivity analyses. The per-patient effect is the mean over that patient's sections, and the reported estimate is the mean over patients with a percentile interval. A naive bootstrap over pairs is reported alongside, to show what ignoring the spatial dependence would have claimed. The analysis was repeated omitting each patient in turn (Supplementary Table S10). Unmatched and matched results are reported together, as in the single-cell analysis.

Statistics

Tests were two-sided. The unmatched contrast is reported alongside the matched contrast throughout so that the effect of each correction is visible. No P value is used in place of an effect estimate, confidence interval or non-estimable result.

Results

CLEC10A is associated with survival in two of three cohorts, and the discrepancy is explained by MYCN status

Cohort characteristics are summarised in Table 1. Overall-survival analysis included 269 tumours and 75 deaths in GSE85047, 498 tumours and 105 deaths in GSE62564, and 153 tumours and 79 deaths in TARGET-NBL. Median-split curves separated in GSE85047 (logrank P=0.013) and GSE62564 (P<0.001) but not TARGET-NBL (P=0.557; Supplementary Fig. S1A-C). Continuous models agreed. Each 1-SD increase in CLEC10A was associated with lower mortality in GSE85047 (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51-0.85, P=0.0016) and GSE62564 (HR 0.56, 0.48-0.66, P=3.4×10 ¹²) but not in TARGET-NBL (HR 0.90, 0.72-1.13, P=0.35). The pooled ⁻ random-effects estimate was 0.69 (0.52-0.92, P=0.011), but with substantial heterogeneity (I²=82%; Fig. 1A). After adjustment for age, stage and MYCN status the estimates attenuated to 0.98 (0.74-1.31), 0.83 (0.68-1.02) and 0.88 (0.68-1.13), pooling to 0.88 (0.76-1.01, P=0.063, I²=0%). CLEC10A is therefore not an independent prognostic variable.

The three cohorts differ markedly in composition (Table 1). TARGET-NBL comprises 82% stage 4 tumours, 81% patients aged ≥18 months and 83% high-risk disease, against 37%, 39% and 48% in GSE62564, and 52% of TARGET patients died versus 21% in GSE62564. This raised the possibility that the discrepancy reflects who is in each cohort rather than whether the association is real.

Table 1. Characteristics of the three neuroblastoma cohorts. Characteristic GSE85047 GSE62564 TARGET-NBL Patients, n 269 498 153 Deaths, n (%) 75 (28) 105 (21) 79 (52) Median follow-up of survivors, years 5.3 6.5 9.1 Maximum follow-up, years 17.7 18.1 14.7 Age ≥18 months, n (%) 128 (48) 193 (39) 124 (81) Stage 4, n (%) 123 (46) 183 (37) 126 (82) MYCN amplified, n (%)ᵃ 55 (21) 92 (19) 33 (22) High risk, n (%)ᵇ not recorded 239 (48) 127 (83) MYCN non-amplified, n (deaths) 212 (37) 401 (53) 119 (60) MYCN amplified, n (deaths) 55 (37) 92 (51) 33 (18)

MYCN status was missing for 2 patients in GSE85047, 5 in GSE62564 and 1 in TARGETᵃ NBL; percentages are of patients with a recorded status. Risk group was not available in ᵇ GSE85047 and was therefore excluded from the primary adjusted model (Methods).

Stratifying by MYCN status resolved the discrepancy (Fig. 1B). In MYCN non-amplified tumours the hazard ratio was 0.74 (0.52-1.04) in GSE85047, 0.67 (0.50-0.90) in GSE62564 and 0.89 (0.68-1.18) in TARGET-NBL, pooling to 0.77 (0.65-0.91, P=0.003) with no detectable heterogeneity (I²=0%). In MYCN-amplified tumours the corresponding estimates were 1.03 (0.65-1.62), 0.94 (0.72-1.21) and 1.08 (0.63-1.83), pooling to 0.98 (0.79-1.20, P=0.82, I²=0%). The heterogeneity present in the overall analysis (I²=82%) was thus no longer detectable after stratification, and TARGET-NBL -the cohort in which the association had appeared to fail -behaved like the others once its MYCN non-amplified patients were considered separately. These pooled intervals should not be read as firmly as their width suggests. The betweenstudy variance was estimated as zero in every stratum, so the random-effects estimate is numerically the fixed-effect estimate, and the normal-based interval treats a variance estimated from three studies as if it were known. Substituting the modified Knapp-Hartung estimator, which uses a t quantile on two degrees of freedom and does not allow the variance to shrink below its fixed-effect value, leaves the point estimates unchanged and widens the intervals substantially: 0.77 (0.53-1.12, P=0.097) in MYCN non-amplified tumours, 0.98 (0.62-1.54, P=0.84) in amplified tumours, and 1.36 (0.73-2.54, P=0.165) for the unadjusted interaction (Supplementary Table S9). The unmodified estimator behaves differently in two of the three strata: because the between-study variance is zero and the weighted residual mean square is below one, it rescales the variance downward and so narrows rather than widens the interval, to 0.98 (0.83-1.15, P=0.60) in amplified tumours and 1.36 (1.13-1.65, P=0.020) for the interaction. We report the modified form throughout because a variance estimate from three studies should not be allowed to make an interval narrower than the fixed-effect one. The non-amplified estimate also depends on one cohort: of the three, only GSE62564 reaches significance within the stratum (HR 0.67, P=0.007; GSE85047 P=0.087, TARGET-NBL P=0.423), and omitting it moves the pooled estimate to 0.83 (0.67-1.03, P=0.090). We therefore report the direction and consistency of the stratified estimates as the finding, and treat the effect modification by MYCN as suggestive rather than established.

Within-cohort interaction tests were individually underpowered (ratio of hazard ratios 1.39, 1.42 and 1.22; P=0.256, 0.078 and 0.519), but pooling them gave a consistent and statistically supported effect: 1.36 (1.03-1.81, P=0.032) unadjusted and 1.36 (1.01-1.82, P=0.044) after adjustment for age and stage, with I²=0% in both cases (Fig. 1C); no single cohort reaches nominal significance on its own (Supplementary Fig. S2E). Pooled Kaplan-Meier display shows the same pattern (non-amplified: n=732, 150 deaths, log-rank P=0.008; amplified: n=180, 106 deaths, P=0.521; Fig. 1D), as do the within-cohort mediansplit tests (Supplementary Fig. S2F).

The immune contrast associated with MYCN was broader than CLEC10A alone. Eleven of 12 prespecified genes were meta-estimable and all were lower in MYCN-amplified tumours (Supplementary Fig. S2A; TRAC was absent or invariant in two cohorts and is shown for TARGET-NBL only in Supplementary Fig. S2C). Random-effects module estimates were -0.86 (-1.13 to -0.59) for antigen presentation and -0.82 (-1.12 to -0.52) for the T-cellinflamed module (Supplementary Fig. S2B), and both were lower in every cohort taken separately (Supplementary Fig. S2D). These are observational contrasts and do not establish direct MYCN-mediated suppression of any of these genes.

CLEC10A detection in single cells is confounded by sequencing depth and cell-type composition

The myeloid/APC compartment of GSE147766 contained 8,219 cells from 17 biological patients, of which 8,092 cells from 14 patients were MYCN non-amplified. As expected, the patient-level fraction of CLEC10A-positive cells was highest in cDC2-like cells (median 78.1%) and near zero in cDC1-like cells (median 0%, four of the six evaluable patients having none; 0.4% of all cDC1-like cells), supporting the specificity of the marker (Fig. 2A-B).

Two features of the data make the conventional CLEC10A-positive versus negative contrast unsafe. First, because cDC2-like cells are a minority of the myeloid compartment, only 18% of CLEC10A-positive cells were cDC2-like; the largest contributors were migratory DC (57%) and monocytes/macrophages (18%), and the composition of the positive and negative pools differed substantially (Fig. 2C). A naive contrast therefore partly measures cell identity rather than cell state. Second, CLEC10A-positive cells were more deeply sequenced than CLEC10A-negative cells in every patient examined (median UMI ratio 1.48, paired Wilcoxon P=0.0002, 13/13 patients; Fig. 2D), and within-patient logistic regression gave an odds ratio for CLEC10A detection of 2.48 (2.28-2.70) per 1-SD higher log UMI (P=4×10 ; Supplementary Fig. S3A).

⁻⁹⁶

Matching each CLEC10A-positive cell to a depth-matched CLEC10A-negative cell of the same subtype and the same patient produced 1,216 matched pairs across 14 patients, of which 13 patients and 1,214 pairs met the pre-set requirement of at least 10 matched cells per group (pairs by subtype in Supplementary Fig. S4C) and entered the differential expression, and removed the depth imbalance (cell-level median UMI 4,003 versus 4,037; patient-level paired Wilcoxon P=0.27). The consequences were substantial. The number of genes significant at FDR<0.05 fell from 395 to 107 (Supplementary Fig. S3B-C; full results in Supplementary Tables S5 and S1), and the strongest positive Hallmark signal of the unmatched analysis, MYC targets v1, collapsed from NES 2.14 (q<0.001) to NES 1.29 (q=0.83) (Supplementary Fig. S3D; Supplementary Table S4).

Matching alters four things at once -sequencing depth, subtype composition, the number of cells compared, and through that the genes surviving independent filtering -so we separated them, running the same patient-paired model on the same cells under five designs and scoring each identically (Methods; Supplementary Table S11). Reducing the negatives to the number of positives alone took the significant gene count from 395 to a median of 289 over five seeds; matching on subtype alone gave 207, on depth alone 157, and on both 113, close to the 107 obtained with the single seed used for the reported analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3E). The fall in gene count is therefore not attributable to any one of the three.

The MYC-target signal behaves differently, and its attribution is unambiguous. Scored as a competitive rank test of the gene set against all other tested genes, it was +6.9 in the unmatched contrast, +5.2 with cell number alone controlled, +3.7 with subtype alone and +2.0 with depth alone; adding subtype on top of depth changed nothing further (+2.3). Essentially all of it is attributable to sequencing depth, and we therefore describe the enrichment of MYC targets in CLEC10A-positive APCs as an artefact of library depth. The MHC class II signal was the one quantity invariant to every correction: +7.0 unmatched, and +7.1 to +7.2 under each of the four matched designs.

After matching, CLEC10A marks an MHC class II-high, alarmin-low myeloid state

The signal that survived matching was coherent. Of the 106 differentially expressed genes other than CLEC10A itself, 72 were higher in CLEC10A-positive cells and 34 lower, and seven of the eight most significant upregulated genes were MHC class II -HLA-DPB1, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DPA1, HLA-DRA, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DMA -the eighth being HCST. The two remaining class II genes in the tested set, CD74 and HLA-DRB5, were also significant, ranked 18th and 33rd of the 72. The genes lower in CLEC10A-positive cells were dominated by the S100 alarmin and inflammatory monocyte programme: S100A8, STXBP2, CCL4, S100A9 and FCGR3A were all significant and are the first, second, third, fourth and eighth most significant of the 34. Two further members of that programme moved in the same direction without reaching significance -SERPINA1 (log -0.40, ₂ q=0.07) and S100A12 (log -1.14), the latter not passing independent filtering (Fig. 2E).

₂

The MHC class II module score was higher in CLEC10A-positive cells in 13 of 13 patients (median log ratio 0.35, paired Wilcoxon P=0.0002), and the S100 module was lower in 11 ₂ of 13 (median log ratio -0.36, P=0.002). Critically, both effects were reproduced within ₂ monocytes/macrophages alone -7 of 7 patients for MHC class II (log 0.52, P=0.016) and ₂ 6 of 7 for S100 (log -0.61, P=0.031) -establishing that the state is intrinsic to a single ₂ myeloid cell type and cannot be explained by cDC2 admixture. In migratory DC the same directions were seen but did not reach significance (5 of 7, P=0.109; 4 of 7, P=0.375; Fig. 2F, Supplementary Fig. S4A).

Gene-set enrichment on the matched contrast, after removal of ribosomal protein genes, ranked MHC class II antigen processing and presentation first among positively enriched terms (NES 2.16, q=0.011), followed by presentation of exogenous antigen (NES 2.03, q=0.042), positive regulation of T-cell-mediated immunity (NES 1.86, q=0.145), positive regulation of leukocyte-mediated cytotoxicity (NES 1.83, q=0.156) and interferon-γ mediated signalling (NES 1.82, q=0.149). Negatively enriched terms were neutrophil degranulation (NES -2.10, q=0.011), neutrophil-mediated immunity (NES -2.11, q=0.019), regulation of complement activation (NES -2.07, q=0.007) and iron ion transport (NES -1.95, q=0.034). Notably, antigen processing and presentation via MHC class I ran in the opposite direction to class II (NES -1.93, q=0.030), indicating that CLEC10A-positive cells are not globally antigen-presentation-high but specifically class II-high (Fig. 2G). Omitting each patient in turn preserved the direction of every one of the 106 significant non-CLEC10A genes (sign concordance 1.00 in all 13 leave-one-patient-out fits; Supplementary Fig. S4B).

Repeating the identical pipeline on all patients rather than the MYCN non-amplified subset gave the same result (Supplementary Fig. S5; full results in Supplementary Table S2). That scope yielded 1,232 matched pairs across 15 patients, of which 14 patients and 1,230 pairs met the same minimum of 10 matched cells per group, 120 differentially expressed genes excluding CLEC10A, and the same MHC class II-dominated top set; log fold changes ₂ correlated across the two scopes at r=0.986 and all 106 genes significant in the primary analysis retained their direction. Gene-set enrichment was also preserved, with MHC class II antigen processing and presentation the strongest term (NES 2.36, q<0.001) and translation-related terms remaining weak (q≥0.08), confirming that the depth correction holds in the wider scope.

In tissue, CLEC10A-positive myeloid bins occupy T-cell-richer neighbourhoods, and this survives depth matching

Having established what CLEC10A marks within a cell, we asked where those cells sit. Six Visium HD sections from five patients met the prespecified immune-content criteria, comprising 53,433 to 166,127 in-tissue bins each at 8 µm resolution (Supplementary Table S7); one section is shown in Fig. 3A.

The same depth confound operates on the spatial data. The probability that an 8 µm bin was called T-cell positive rose with bin sequencing depth in five of the six sections, the ratio between the highest and the lowest depth quintile ranging from 0.97 to 10.1 (Fig. 3B), and bin depth was spatially autocorrelated, predicting the mean depth of the surrounding 48 µm ring at Spearman 0.783-0.891 and of a 24 µm ring at 0.871-0.942 (Supplementary ρ Fig. S6A). Outcomes built on T-cell detection are therefore partly depth-driven, and the natural choice -distance to the nearest T-cell-positive bin -is on an 8 µm lattice additionally confined to a small set of discrete values (8.0, 11.3, 16.0, 17.9, 22.6 µm; Supplementary Fig. S6B), so group medians can fall only on those values and coincided in four of the six sections after matching (Supplementary Fig. S6D). We therefore used a depth-normalised outcome: T-cell transcripts per 1,000 UMI within 48 µm of each bin, excluding the bin itself. CLEC10A positivity is itself a detection call, so each CLEC10Apositive myeloid bin was matched within section to a CLEC10A-negative myeloid bin on myeloid count and log total UMI; matching equalised the depth of the neighbourhood as well as of the bin (ratio of mean neighbourhood UMI 0.963-1.003, Supplementary Fig. S6E). The unmatched comparisons are reported alongside the matched ones throughout (Supplementary Fig. S6C,F).

Neighbourhoods of 48 µm overlap -70% to 100% of analysed bins per section lie within 96 µm, twice the neighbourhood radius, of another analysed bin -and two of the six sections come from one patient. Inference is therefore at the level of the patient, with intervals from a spatial block bootstrap over contiguous tiles nested inside a bootstrap over patients (Methods).

The paired difference was positive in all six sections and in all five patients. Per section, the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the paired difference and its block-bootstrap interval were 0.034 (0.003 to 0.078) for SJNBL030875, 0.006 (-0.008 to 0.024) for SJNBL032130, 0.016 (-0.006 to 0.041) for SJNBL033392, 0.018 (-0.004 to 0.039) for SJNBL033392D4, 0.006 (-0.025 to 0.022) for SJNBL066148 and 0.191 (0.084 to 0.307) for SJNBL071611 T-cell transcripts per 1,000 UMI (Fig. 3C). Pooled over the five patients, the difference was 0.051 (95% bootstrap interval 0.003 to 0.134), and the estimate was stable to the choice of tile size between 96 µm and 400 µm. Ignoring the spatial dependence would have made these intervals 1.3 to 2.2 times narrower than they are.

The pooled interval excludes zero, but only narrowly and only with all five patients present. The effect is dominated by SJNBL071611, and omitting any one of three patients brings zero inside the interval (Supplementary Table S10). What the data support is a consistent direction across five patients, not a reliably estimated magnitude.

Matching equalised not only each bin's own depth but the depth of its neighbourhood, the ratio of mean neighbourhood UMI between CLEC10A-positive bins and their matched controls lying between 0.963 and 1.003 across sections, so the groups are balanced on neighbourhood depth as well as on their own. Balance of the mean does not establish balance of the distribution, and residual confounding through local composition is not excluded. The one section without a difference, SJNBL066148, is also the section in which myeloid-positive bins make up 59.6% of tissue and CLEC10A-positive bins are an order of magnitude more numerous than elsewhere (1,697 versus 149-343); where myeloid cells are distributed throughout the tissue there is little positional contrast left to detect. These data place the CLEC10A-associated myeloid state in T-cell-richer tissue, measured over a fixed physical radius and with the depth confound addressed. They do not show that these myeloid cells prime, activate or recruit T cells; co-location at 8 µm is compatible with any of those and with none of them.

Discussion

CLEC10A has been read in neuroblastoma, as elsewhere, as a count of cDC2 [14, 19, 20]. These data indicate that in tumour tissue it is better read as a marker of a state. Once the two artefacts that dominate marker-positive versus marker-negative comparisons are removed, what CLEC10A identifies is an MHC class II-high, alarmin-low transcriptional programme that is present across myeloid cell types rather than confined to one lineage, that occupies T-cell-richer tissue, and whose association with survival appears only where MYCN is not amplified.

The state is not a property of which broad cell types are present. CLEC10A-positive myeloid cells are MHC class II-high and S100 alarmin-low, and both directions reproduce within monocytes and macrophages considered alone -class II in 7 of 7 patients, S100 in 6 of 7 -so the signal cannot be explained by cDC2 admixture, and indeed only 18% of CLEC10A-positive cells were cDC2-like. Monocytes and macrophages are themselves heterogeneous [22], so this does not exclude every compositional explanation; it excludes the one the marker invites. The accompanying reductions in complement and neutrophillike inflammatory programmes argue for a specific phenotype rather than generic activation. Being alarmin-low is itself informative, because S100A8, S100A9 and S100A12 define the inflammatory monocyte programme that characterises suppressive myeloid states [39, 40]; the CLEC10A-associated state runs against that programme rather than with it. The module we scored is broader than the three alarmins, so this is a statement about the programme as a whole.

That this is a class II programme carries more weight in neuroblastoma than it would in most tumours. Neuroblastoma presents poorly through MHC class I. Its somatic mutation burden is among the lowest of any cancer, so few neoantigens are available [7], and class I expression on tumour cells is low, a defect tied to MYCN amplification in work from 1986 [8]. Where class I presentation is constrained, the class II-CD4 axis is what remains, and MHC class II-restricted help can by itself drive protective antitumour immunity [17]. A readout of intratumoural class II capacity is therefore of more than descriptive interest here. One feature of the state points the same way and was not anticipated: antigen processing and presentation via MHC class I ran in the opposite direction to class II within the same cells. Whether that reflects a division of labour inside the myeloid compartment, or the same pressures that lower class I on neuroblastoma cells acting on myeloid cells as well, cannot be settled from one dataset; we offer it as a hypothesis for replication rather than as a finding.

In tissue, this state is found where T cells are. At 8 µm resolution, CLEC10A-positive myeloid bins occupy neighbourhoods richer in T-cell transcripts than myeloid bins matched for sequencing depth and myeloid content, in all six sections and all five patients. The direction is the robust part. The magnitude is not: one patient contributes most of it, the pooled interval excludes zero only when all five are present, and with five patients a bootstrap interval is itself a rough instrument. The claim is correspondingly narrow -the state is positioned near T cells rather than away from them. Proximity within a 48 µm radius is not contact, a bin is not a cell, and nothing here shows that anything passes between them.

The survival association behaves in a way that fits this reading, and in doing so resolves an apparent inconsistency. Taken cohort by cohort CLEC10A looks unreliable: the association is clear in GSE85047 and in GSE62564 and absent in TARGET-NBL. That is a composition effect. TARGET-NBL is heavily enriched for high-risk and stage 4 disease (Table 1), and once the three cohorts are stratified by MYCN status the between-cohort heterogeneity is no longer detectable (I² from 82% to 0%) and the estimates align in direction. How strongly that can be asserted is limited by having three cohorts: the between-study variance is estimated as zero, so the random-effects interval is really a fixed-effect interval, and an estimator that prices in the uncertainty of that variance widens the stratum estimate to 0.77 (0.53-1.12) and the interaction to 1.36 (0.73-2.54). Within the nonamplified stratum only GSE62564 is individually significant. The consistent direction across three cohorts and two strata is the substance of the result; the effect modification itself is suggestive, and we do not claim it as established. It remains true that CLEC10A is not independently prognostic after clinical adjustment, and we do not propose it as a standalone biomarker. Its potential use is different in kind: a readout, available in the bulk datasets that most neuroblastoma cohorts consist of, of an immune property that singlecell work can otherwise measure in only a handful of patients. This reading converges with, rather than contradicts, the annotation adopted in the harmonised neuroblastoma single-cell reference atlas [14]. That atlas calls cDC2 by CD1C, CD1E and CLEC10A, which is the conventional use of the marker, but it also places a separate CLEC10A-expressing population inside the monocyte compartment, annotated as monocytes in transition to macrophages. This is not independent replication: the dataset re-analysed here [15] is one of the seven studies NBAtlas integrates, and with 19 of its 68 samples it is the largest single contributor. What it does show is that the assignment survives a different annotation pipeline applied to a corpus six times larger, rather than being a product of how we annotated these cells. What a reference atlas is not built to establish -its purpose being to assign identity rather than to contrast states within oneis what CLEC10A expression means functionally inside those cells; the atlas does not link CLEC10A to MHC class II at any point, attributing the highest HLA expression instead to a FOLR2-positive macrophage population of the kind associated with T-cell infiltration in other tumours [42]. One point in that annotation deserves comment, because it runs against our interpretation and would otherwise be left open. The atlas names IDO1 and LGALS2 alongside CLEC10A among the genes marking its CLEC10A-expressing monocyte cluster [14], and IDO1 is immunoregulatory [43]; if CLEC10A tracked IDO1 at the single-cell level, a class II-high, T-cell-supportive reading would be hard to sustain. In these data it does not. IDO1 was not higher in CLEC10A-positive cells even in the naive contrast, in which the depth confound biases genes upward (log fold change -0.71, P=0.30), and was ₂ too sparsely detected to test after matching; LGALS2 was nominally higher before matching (log 0.73, P=0.009) but not after it (log 0.58, P=0.12) and was flat within monocytes and ₂ ₂ macrophages alone (log 0.02, P=0.96). Of the markers the atlas assigns to that cluster, only ₂ the MHC class II transcripts it does not assign to CLEC10A survive depth matching.

These observations form a single axis. The prespecified antigen-presentation module is lower in MYCN-amplified tumours; CLEC10A marks an MHC class II-high myeloid state at the single-cell level; that state sits where T cells are; and the survival association attached to CLEC10A is present only where the immune context is preserved -in MYCN nonamplified disease. The parsimonious interpretation is that CLEC10A is a readout of intratumoural class II antigen-presentation capacity, and that this capacity carries prognostic information only when MYCN amplification has not already dictated the outcome.

What this chain does not contain is the step that would make it mechanistic. We have a prognostic association stratified by MYCN, a cell state defined at single-cell resolution with its two main artefacts removed, and a spatial relationship between that state and T cells. We do not have evidence that these myeloid cells present antigen to, activate, or expand T cells. That step cannot be supplied by any of the public data used here: co-location is not interaction, transcript is not protein, and an association across tumours is not a demonstration of causation within one. It requires functional work, and we regard it as the central open question rather than a detail to be filled in later. CLEC10A is also not an inert marker. Its ligand is terminal N-acetylgalactosamine, including the tumour-associated Tn antigen [18], and engagement of CD45 on T cells by the receptor has been shown to attenuate effector T-cell responses [44]. A receptor that marks antigen-presentation capacity while also being able to restrain the T cells it meets is not a contradiction, but it does mean that the sign of any functional effect cannot be read off expression. Our claim concerns what CLEC10A expression marks on myeloid cells, not what ligation of the receptor does, and the two should not be conflated.

One methodological point bears statement, because it determines whether results of this kind can be believed. Grouping cells by detection of a marker makes sequencing depth a determinant of the exposure rather than of the outcome: here the odds of being called CLEC10A-positive rose 2.5-fold per standard deviation of log depth, and because the marker is enriched in one subtype the two pools differed in composition as well. Covariate adjustment of the kind MAST performs [30] cannot repair a contrast already formed on a depth-dependent split. The consequences were not subtle -395 significant genes and a strong MYC-target signature before matching, 107 genes and no MYC-target enrichment after. Running the same model under designs that control depth, composition and cell number separately shows that the MYC-target signal tracks depth alone, that the genecount drop reflects all three, and that the MHC class II signal moves under none of them; attribution of this kind is worth doing, because matching changes several things at once and the naive reading is that it changed only the one the analyst had in mind. The same mechanism operated on the spatial data, where a detection-based proximity outcome was depth-driven until it was replaced by one normalised to local depth. Because spatial and single-cell data are increasingly used to make proximity claims about marker-defined populations [41, 42], we report the naive and corrected contrasts side by side throughout and would encourage the same practice. The survival analysis makes a parallel point: where cohorts differ in clinical composition, stratified meta-analysis is more informative than counting significant and non-significant cohorts. Several limitations apply. All analyses are retrospective and observational; the cohorts differ in platform and in the covariates available, and adjustment attenuates the survival association (Supplementary Fig. S1E). The proportional-hazards assumption is violated for the CLEC10A term in GSE62564 and, univariably, in TARGET-NBL (Supplementary Fig. S1F), so the hazard ratios we report should be read as time-averaged effects rather than constant ones; because almost all deaths occur within five years the estimates are nevertheless stable across follow-up horizons (Supplementary Fig. S1G). We show that MYCN status modifies the CLEC10A-survival relationship, but not that MYCN suppresses CLEC10A or class II presentation directly. The single-cell analysis rests on 13 patient pairs from one atlas, MYCN-amplified tumours contributed too few APCs for a paired contrast, and a cDC2-restricted analysis was underpowered (4 eligible patients). One sample, NB37, is classified as MYCN non-amplified by the source study's annotation, which we followed, but as amplified in the reference atlas, which assigns status by inference; it contributes 318 of the 8,092 cells in the scope and only 2 matched pairs, so it is excluded from the differential expression by the minimum-cell rule and cannot affect that result, but the scope statement depends on which annotation is taken. Matching necessarily discards unmatched cells and can only balance the confounders that are measured; residual differences in RNA content or capture efficiency may persist.

The spatial analysis carries its own limits. It rests on six sections from five patients, one patient contributing two; MYCN status is not recorded in the source annotation, so the spatial result could not be stratified by the variable that organises the rest of this study; an 8 µm bin contains one to a few cells, so a bin is not a cell and adjacency is not contact; the Visium HD probe panel covers 18,132 genes rather than the whole transcriptome; the pooled interval excludes zero only with all five patients present and is dominated by one of them, and a bootstrap interval built on five units is a rough instrument; and the dataset had no associated publication at the time of analysis, so it is cited by accession only. Finally, transcript detection is not protein abundance, and none of these data demonstrate function.

The obvious next steps follow from those limits. Flow or mass cytometry should test whether CLEC10A-positive tumour myeloid cells carry higher surface HLA-DR protein and lower S100A8/A9, in MYCN-amplified as well as non-amplified tumours. Because our claim is that CLEC10A marks a functional state rather than that it creates one, the decisive experiment is to sort CLEC10A-positive and CLEC10A-negative myeloid cells and compare their capacity to activate and polarise naive T cells, rather than to force CLEC10A expression, which tests a different proposition. Spatial data at single-cell resolution, and paired T-cell receptor repertoires, would establish whether co-location corresponds to clonal engagement. Until then, CLEC10A is best used as a contextual readout of myeloid class II antigen-presentation capacity in MYCN non-amplified neuroblastoma. , A) is absent within either stratum. Figure2. CLEC10A marks an MHC class II-high, alarmin-low state within tumour myeloid cells. MYCN non-amplified tumours; annotation was defined without CLEC10A. A, Myeloid/APC UMAP. B, Patient-level fraction of CLEC10A-positive cells by subtype, restricted to patients contributing ≥20 cells of that subtype; n is the number of such patients. C, Subtype composition of CLEC10A-negative and CLEC10A-positive cells; despite the highest detection rate in cDC2-like cells, only 18% of CLEC10A-positive cells are cDC2like. D, Median UMI per cell by CLEC10A status, before and after matching; each line is one patient. E, Depth-and subtype-matched, biological-patient-paired pseudobulk differential expression (13 patient pairs, 1,216 matched cell pairs). CLEC10A is excluded because it defines the groups. Labelled genes are the most significant members of each highlighted set, placed in a column with leader lines to their points. F, Patient-level MHC class II and S100/inflammatory module scores, overall and within single subtypes; numbers below each group give patients concordant with the overall direction and the paired Wilcoxon P. G, Pre-ranked gene-set enrichment on the matched contrast after removal of ribosomal protein genes; GO term names are abbreviated and given in full in Supplementary TableS3. FDR, false-discovery rate; NES, normalised enrichment score.
